study.title: 1 Samuel 3 The call of Samuel and the judgment on the house of Eli
study.overview: The chapter shows the passage from a period of lack of revelation to a new moment when God speaks clearly with Israel through Samuel. The child, who was already in the sanctuary under the supervision of Eli, hears the voice of the LORD, learns to respond with reverence and receives a harsh message against Eli's house. The narrative highlights both God's holiness in judging persistent sin and his mercy by raising a faithful prophet to lead his people.

outline.title: Lance scarcity and the initial call
outline.explanation: The first verses describe a time of rare divine revelations. Samuel serves at the sanctuary while vision is unusual in Israel. The LORD calls him repeatedly, and Samuel still does not recognize the voice of God; Eli finally realizes that the initiative comes from the Lord.

outline.title: The message against Eli and Samuel's reply
outline.explanation: Eli guides Samuel to place himself as a servant available before God. The LORD announces judgment against Eli's house because of the known and unrebuked guilt, especially for the corruption of Eli's children. Samuel fears to communicate the vision, but then fully transmits it, and Eli submits to divine judgment.

outline.title: Confirmation of the Prophet in Israel
outline.explanation: God accompanies Samuel in his maturity, validating his words. Israel acknowledges that Samuel is the faithful prophet of the LORD, and the text concludes by stating that God has again manifested himself in Shiloh through the word revealed to Samuel.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the sanctuary in Shiloh and Samuel's service under the direction of Eli. There is no broad historical details of external dates or events in the text; the immediate context is the spiritual decay of Eli's leadership and the need for new divine communication with Israel.
study.theology: The text teaches that the revelation of God is not controlled by religious routine; it is the sovereign gift of the LORD. The lack of vision and word is presented as a sign of spiritual crisis, but God does not abandon his people: he calls a young servant, trains him to listen and raises through him a reliable prophetic voice. At the same time, divine holiness demands judgment on deliberate sin and omitted leadership. The refusal of atonement for Eli's house points out that sacrifices do not replace repentance or nullify persistent and rebellious guilt. It is also seen that the true prophet does not speak to please men, but to faithfully convey the message received, even if it is painful.

scholarViews.insight: The observation that the word of the LORD was rare highlights a period of spiritual darkness, about to end when God begins to speak to Samuel.
Samuel appears as an example of diligent service, even young, contrasting with the infidelity of Eli's sons.
Samuel's triple call shows how God prepares him to recognize a special revelation; the prophet's correct answer is reverent availability.

questions: How can I distinguish between religious activity and true attention to God's voice in the Word?
Is there any area in which, like Eli, I was omitted to correcting known sin under my responsibility?
Is my posture in the face of difficult messages of Scripture submission, like that of Eli at the end of the chapter?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to cultivate spiritual ear: set aside time to listen to the Word, respond promptly and not harden the heart before divine warnings. He also exhorts parents, leaders, and disciples not to tolerate known sin, but to act responsibly and repentance. For the life of the church, concrete application is to seek fidelity more than appearance, trusting that God continues to speak for his Word and forming servants who transmit his will with truth and reverence.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail the location of Shiloh or provide additional external historical data; therefore, any magnification beyond what the chapter and the notes say should not be taken as sure. Adam Clarke's text suggests readings about shrine arrangements and religious education, but this should be understood as an interpretation of the commentator, not as explicit data from the chapter.
